newsitem.title: CHINA: Thai offshore bonds upbeat after float, FRNs mixed.
newsitem.headline: Thai offshore bonds upbeat after float, FRNs mixed.

text.p: Dollar bonds of Thai issuers face a brighter future following the government's decision to float the baht, but the outlook for floating rate notes issued by Thai banks is less certain, analysts said on Thursday.

Traders in Hong Kong said prices for Thai fixed-rate paper eased slightly in Asia on profit-taking following strong overnight gains, but spreads were still tighter than indicated before the central bank's action.

"We're seeing some selling now, but I would generally expect that the bonds would tighten in because the currency float removes a major source of uncertainty for the market and in general is good for the export sector," said Raja V, research director at BA Asia in Hong Kong.

Thailand's sovereign Yankee bond due in 2007 tightened to 92-95 basis points over comparable U.S. Treasuries in New York trade from the 105 basis-point level recorded before Thailand's move on the baht, traders said.

The Bank of Thailand announced on Wednesday that it would allow its currency to fluctuate under a managed float system, with its value to be determined by market forces. The baht had been fixed on a daily basis against a basket of currencies dominated by the U.S. dollar.

The move caused the baht to drop some 15-20 percent on Wednesday. It was modestly softer in thin activity on Thursday, trading at 29.00/29.30 to the dollar in the offshore market and 28.00/29.00 in the domestic market in the afternoon.

Thai stocks have soared in response to the currency float, buoyed by views that the de facto devaluation would aid the economy by making Thai exports more competitive and paving the way for interest rate cuts.
That same optimism spurred buying of bonds, traders said.

"Generally the whole Thai government-linked curve tightened 5-7 basis points at the close of New York trading, but it is still too soon to say whether this is a trend," said a syndicate manager in Hong Kong, citing Industrial Finance Corp of Thailand and PTT Exploration and Production.
In Asia, trade in the bonds was thin and erratic, he said.
The even more illiquid floating rate note market has shown little reaction to the news, and traders said the outlook for these issues, which are mostly from banks, is mixed.
Some traders said they believed that, like the bonds, the banks' floating rate notes would benefit from an improved outlook for Thailand's economy.
"I believe the Thai paper is on a tightening track," said a trader at a U.S. commercial bank.
But others worried that the devaluation could increase Thai banks' foreign exchange losses and therefore make their debt issues less attractive.
Banking analysts said it was difficult to determine Thai banks' foreign exchange exposure because many of them borrow dollars and then quickly onlend them to Thai corporations.

As a result, the banks themselves may not have that much dollar exposure, but their clients might have quite a bit. If the burden were to become too much for their clients, the banks could find themselves with more bad loans on their books.

"We're concerned not about the currency exposure of the banks but the credit risk implicit in the baht devaluation because of the foreign exchange risk of the banks' customers, many of which we strongly suspect are unhedged," said Andrew Brown, banking analyst at Salomon Brothers.
"It is difficult to measure this exposure, but we think it is material," he said.
Banks may also face a credit crunch in coming months if it becomes difficult for them to roll over short-dated paper as it matures, bankers noted.
